# Preface {.unnumbered}

## Why This Book

Generative AI invites us to ask what computers can create. Putting it to useful work asks something more demanding: what should a system produce, what evidence should support its output, and who is responsible when that output shapes a decision? A convincing answer on a screen is only the beginning. Understanding its origins, testing its limits, and deciding how it belongs in a larger system require sustained attention.

I wrote this book to connect those questions. Generative AI is a technical discipline, an engineering practice, and a set of decisions about evidence, risk, and responsibility. Learning to prompt a chatbot can be a useful starting point, but it does not resolve questions about retrieval, integration, evaluation, governance, or deployment. Those questions become unavoidable when a demonstration turns into something people depend on.

The aim is to help you explain and defend your choices. Why this model? Why this source of information? What should the assistant be allowed to do? What would count as evidence that it works? These questions give technical learning a purpose. They also encourage a habit that matters throughout the book: treating a plausible result as something to investigate, rather than the end of the inquiry.

## What This Book Covers

The fifteen chapters form five Parts. Part I, Foundations of Generative AI, establishes the conceptual basis for understanding generative models, language models, and prompting. It connects the behavior readers encounter at an interface with ideas about how models represent information and produce responses. That foundation provides a vocabulary for comparing capabilities and recognizing limitations.

Part II, Building Generative AI Systems, moves outward from the model to the application. APIs and integration, agents, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning introduce decisions about information flow, autonomy, and customization. The central concern is how these choices fit a particular problem, including the constraints and responsibilities that come with it.

Part III, Research, Modalities, and Evaluation, asks how to ground and assess a design. Research methods support informed choices; multimodal capabilities broaden the kinds of information a system can handle. Evaluation and optimization bring attention to evidence, performance, cost, and latency. Together, these topics help turn preferences into decisions that can be examined and tested.

Part IV, Responsible Generative AI, considers safety, alignment, ethics, law, and governance. These topics are connected to the engineering decisions that precede them: whose information is used, which actions are permitted, how failures are detected, and who can challenge an outcome. Part V, Production and the Frontier, brings the work toward deployment while considering emerging directions and the uncertainty that accompanies them.

## Learning by Designing

A sustained project runs through the book: the design of an AI-powered research assistant for a domain you choose. Keeping one domain gives each new topic a concrete setting. It also makes the consequences of earlier decisions visible. A model choice affects the integration plan; a retrieval strategy affects evaluation; a proposed autonomous action creates questions for the safety and ethics reviews.

The project develops through a portfolio. You begin with a charter and move through model selection, a prompt library, integration architecture, agent capabilities, retrieval design, and a customization decision. Research grounding, a multimodal extension plan, evaluation, and optimization add further reasoning. Red-team, ethics, compliance, and deployment work complete the arc. Each contribution should explain both the choice and the reasons behind it.

Understanding and judgment are the priorities. A working prototype can enrich the work, but it is optional in the project design. A carefully argued architecture, a useful test plan, or a clear account of a system's limits can demonstrate substantial learning. Documentation makes that learning available for discussion: another reader should be able to understand your assumptions, question your evidence, and follow your trade-offs.

## Who This Book Is For

This book is intended for advanced undergraduate and graduate students, instructors, software engineers, data scientists, researchers, AI practitioners, and technical professionals. Readers will bring different levels of experience with programming, machine learning, and system design. The combination of conceptual discussion, technical examples, and design milestones offers several ways to engage with the material.

Students can use the project to connect topics that might otherwise seem separate. Practitioners can bring a concrete application to the chapters and use the questions to examine existing choices. Instructors can adapt the sequence, discussions, and milestones to their course. Across these uses, the common expectation is a willingness to reason carefully, investigate unfamiliar ideas, and make assumptions explicit.

## How to Use This Book

A sequential reading supports the project progression, especially when the material is new. Individual chapters can also serve as references when you need to revisit a specific design question. When reading selectively, look back at the concepts and project decisions on which the chapter depends. A local improvement may have consequences elsewhere in the system.

Use the learning objectives to establish what you are trying to understand, and return to the key terminologies and concepts when a distinction is unclear. Work through examples actively: ask what assumption makes an approach appropriate and what change in context might undermine it. Technical examples are opportunities to trace reasoning as well as to study the mechanics of a technique.

Case studies and discussion questions invite comparison and disagreement supported by evidence. Further Reading provides directions for deeper investigation, while chapter wrap-ups help consolidate the main ideas. The names and arrangement of these learning features vary across chapters. Project milestones give you a place to apply the ideas and preserve your reasoning. Revisit earlier portfolio entries when later material reveals a missing constraint or a better question.

## A Fast-Moving Field

Models, APIs, pricing, regulation, and product names change quickly. A useful education must help readers distinguish durable principles from time-sensitive implementation details. The need to define a task, assess evidence, understand a failure, and assign responsibility remains valuable even as particular tools change.

Read specific examples with attention to their context. Before relying on an implementation detail in your own work, consult the relevant current documentation or primary source and record what you checked. This habit supports reproducibility and makes later revision easier. It also helps keep enthusiasm connected to evidence: the question is what a system can reliably accomplish under the conditions that matter to its users.

## Open Education

Published by Global Data Science Institute, this First Open Edition is available as an open educational resource under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International, or CC BY 4.0. The license supports sharing and adaptation with appropriate attribution. Instructors can adapt material for teaching, and readers can use it as a basis for further study and discussion.

The free online edition, downloadable PDF and EPUB, and public source repository provide different ways to read and work with the book. Open access also makes it easier to examine how ideas are presented and to discuss where explanation or evidence could be strengthened. My hope is that readers finish with more than familiarity with a set of tools: they should be better prepared to ask precise questions, evaluate alternatives, and take responsibility for the systems they help create.
